---
title: Reusable representations
description: "Export learned context as embeddings and evaluate them as inputs to separate predictors."
engine: markdown
---

Suppose you have trained the payment-history model to predict disputes and
now want a separate predictor of merchant-repeat payments. Each dataset row
still describes one account at a review cutoff, using only the history known
then. Export that row's learned context and test it as input to a predictor
with settled merchant-repeat labels, alongside existing spending summaries.
This evaluates reuse without fitting the history model again for the new
task. Each predictor still needs its own labels and held-out assessment.

An embedding is a numeric representation of the context the model has learned.
Set `embed=True` where you want to export one. Exporting adds no learning
objective; use a model already trained with supervision or reconstruction.
It makes the generated model useful as a candidate source of learned
representations as well as task predictions. The comparisons below establish
whether those representations help the new decision.

## Choose where to export

Continue with the saved payment model from
[Pretraining and fine-tuning](pretraining-and-fine-tuning.qmd). It already includes
the account profile and transactions, including the latest payment once. Turn
on exports at its root and `trxns` branch:

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.load("artifacts/payment-disputes.rf")
model.update(
    rf.where("address").is_in(
        [rf.Address(), rf.Address("trxns")]
    ),
    embed=True,
)
```

The transaction dispute targets remain in place. The same prediction
pass can now return their estimates and the context vectors used for a separate
task predictor.

| `embed=True` location | Exported representation |
| --- | --- |
| Root | The root's reduced context. |
| Branch | The branch's reduced context. |
| Leaf | The decoder's pooled context before its datatype output head. |


The pretraining example uses the `xs` preset with one-output reductions. This
therefore exports one vector for the account snapshot and one summary of its
transactions per observation. It does not export one vector per transaction.
A nested branch inside `trxns` would retain those outer transaction positions
when exporting its own summary.

For a separate predictor of transaction outcomes, pair the summary with the
corresponding transaction's fields and label. A leaf embedding can instead
provide a contextual vector at each transaction position.

A leaf embedding is different from its raw input embedding: it can include
ancestor context and visible, aligned sibling fields. A branch embedding
summarizes the inputs controlled by that branch's reduction.

## Read the output

This example uses [prediction output](../reference/prediction-output.qmd),
which keeps representations separate from decoded field results.

Use the same account profile and `trxns` records in your application's request
file, omitting `disputed` from every transaction. The snapshot cutoff remains
the final booking time; all vectors describe the evidence available then.
Export the vectors in prediction mode:

```python
requests = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    predict="payments/finetuning/requests.parquet",
)
result = model.predict(datamodule=requests, batch_size=256, devices=1)
```

Each row's `representations` list holds one record per exported vector. An
empty `path` is the anonymous root, and `["trxns"]` is the transaction
summary. Rows come back in request order:

```python
snapshot_vectors = []
history_vectors = []
for row in result.to_pylist():
    for record in row["representations"]:
        if record["path"] == []:
            snapshot_vectors.append(record["embedding"])
        elif record["path"] == ["trxns"]:
            history_vectors.append(record["embedding"])
```

For many rows, let Polars give you one row per vector, with an `observation`
index that ties each vector back to its request row:

```python
import polars as pl

vectors = (
    pl.from_arrow(result)
    .with_row_index("observation")
    .select("observation", "representations")
    .explode("representations")
    .unnest("representations")
    .with_columns(path=pl.col("path").list.join("/"))
)
snapshot_vectors = vectors.filter(pl.col("path") == "")
history_vectors = vectors.filter(pl.col("path") == "trxns")
```

Field names cannot contain `/`, so joining path segments does not merge
distinct paths.

Exported vectors are float32 and L2-normalized along their fixed `d_model`
axis; zero vectors remain zero. Each representation record also carries
`parents` and `output_index`. If a later schema groups several accounts
inside an `accounts` branch, an `/accounts/trxns`
summary uses `parents=[a]` to select account `a`. For the merchant leaf inside it,
`parents=[a,t]` selects transaction `t` of account `a`. These are retained
coordinates after queries and overflow, including structural holes.

`rf.Attention(n_outputs=3)` produces records with `output_index` 0, 1, and 2 at
each summary site. `reduction=None` preserves the routed output stream,
including its defined zero slots; its output indices do not claim an inferred
source-record identity. A branch summary can exist for an empty collection
when its reduction defines that output. A leaf embedding requires a valid
item coordinate. Representation counts therefore need not match item counts.
See [Branch](../datatypes/branch.qmd) and the full
[Prediction output](../reference/prediction-output.qmd) contract.

Evaluate an embedding on its intended downstream task. A useful dispute
predictor does not by itself establish useful similarity or clustering.
Preserve the schema and trained state with
[the model artifact](../guides/checkpoints-ema-and-resuming.qmd#save-and-load).

To evaluate a frozen representation, keep the exporting model fixed and
generate vectors in prediction mode for the training and held-out
observations. Fit separate task predictors using only the training vectors
and labels. Keep the exporting model fixed throughout: this measures what a
downstream predictor can learn from the representation as exported.

Choose cohort and time boundaries before training. For an evaluation on
unseen accounts, exclude held-out accounts from both representation learning
and downstream predictor training. Each history vector represents the account
at a defined decision cutoff; the task label records an outcome over a later
period. Keep records after that cutoff out of the input snapshot.

Compare existing features alone, vectors alone, and their combination on the
same observations. Choose predictor settings on the same validation split and
assess the fixed choices on test data. For merchant-repeat prediction, measure
precision and recall for the defined 30-day outcome window. For payment review,
measure dispute recall at a fixed review capacity. These task metrics help
decide whether the reusable representation earns a place in the workflow.
[Profile context and a second outcome](profile-context-and-a-second-outcome.qmd)
explains how to prepare the observations and outcome windows for these
experiments.

## Learn without a label

You can export context before adapting to a supervised outcome. Load the
reconstruction-trained artifact from the same payment workflow and request
the root and transaction summaries:

```python
reconstructed = rf.Model.load("artifacts/payment-pretrained.rf")
reconstructed.update(
    rf.where("address").is_in(
        [rf.Address(), rf.Address("trxns")]
    ),
    embed=True,
)
```

The pretraining fit uses sampled transaction amounts and merchants as its
objectives, without dispute labels. Run prediction with that fitted model to
generate vectors for a separately labeled task. `embed=True` alone creates no
objective, and sampled reconstruction does not request ordinary decoded
prediction output. [Masking and reconstruction](../concepts/masking-and-reconstruction.qmd) explains
that distinction. Supervised and sampled reconstruction objectives can coexist,
with each leaf's `weight` scaling its contribution.

[Pretraining and fine-tuning](pretraining-and-fine-tuning.qmd) shows how to transfer
reconstruction training to a labeled task. The
[reconstruction transfer evidence](../evidence/representation/reconstruction-transfer.html)
compares frozen root embeddings with raw features, an untrained encoder, and
training on independently permuted views.

Next, explore [Use cases](../use-cases/index.qmd) to organize forecasting,
recommendations, customer outcomes, and related-record predictions around
their own datasets and decisions. Define and evaluate the representation for
each schema and task before relying on it.
